{"markdown":"# Issues Memo — Master Services Agreement

**To:** Deal team
**From:** In-house counsel (Customer side)
**Re:** Playbook review of Vendor's Master Services Agreement — verified findings

---

## 1. Executive summary

We reviewed the MSA against 19 playbook rules. Eleven clauses are compliant, several of them at the preferred position and clearly in our favour: Customer ownership of Customer Data and Deliverables (§ 14), assignment and change-of-control freedom (§ 24), termination for convenience with refund of prepaid Fees (§ 9.4), a tightly bounded once-yearly audit right with a 5% cost-shift trigger (§ 22), New York law and New York County courts (§ 28), 12-month auto-renewal with a 30-day opt-out and a CPI/3% uplift cap (§ 8), full Vendor insurance including USD 5M cyber (§ 18), and no MFN, no-hire or Customer-payable liquidated damages anywhere in the document.

Eight clauses are deviations, and seven of those fall into walk-away territory. The commercial core of the problem is a cluster of Vendor-favourable terms that are internally inconsistent with the rest of the agreement: a three-year USD 2,000,000 take-or-pay with no reduction or termination rights (§ 2.1), sole-source exclusivity for the full term (§ 2.2), a 24-month post-term non-compete on us (§ 12.4), a Services licence that excludes our Affiliates and contractors and is revocable at Vendor's discretion (§ 13.1), a one-month liability cap applying "without exception" (§ 21.1), a one-way unlimited Customer indemnity with no Vendor indemnity at all (§ 20), immediate deletion of Customer Data with no transition assistance (§ 11.1), and a 15-day Deliverable warranty that extinguishes the otherwise open-ended conformance warranty (§ 19.2).

Several of these provisions contradict clauses elsewhere in the same document — § 12.3 records that we have made no exclusivity, minimum-volume or no-hire commitment; §§ 11.2–11.3 provide for data return before deletion; § 13.3 permits revocation only for uncured material breach; § 21.3 defines Excluded Claims that § 21.1 purports to override. The order-of-precedence provision (the second § 2.2) does not resolve internal conflicts within the Agreement. We should treat the inconsistencies as leverage: in each case the Vendor's own drafting already concedes our position elsewhere.

Drafting defects to raise separately: the Agreement contains two provisions numbered § 2.2, and § 9.3 relies on remedies "required by Section 20.5", which does not exist.

---

## 2. Findings

| # | Rule | Severity | Status | Section | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | IP — Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data | Critical | Compliant | § 14.1 (with §§ 13.2, 14.2–14.4, 15.1) | Preferred position: Customer owns Data and Deliverables; present assignment; no model training without consent. |
| 2 | ASSIGN — Assignment and change of control | High | Compliant | § 24.1 (with §§ 24.2–24.4, 13.3) | Preferred position in full; no Vendor exit or repricing on our change of control. |
| 3 | LD — Liquidated damages payable by Customer | High | Compliant | § 9.4 (with §§ 7.1, 24.4, 27.3) | No Customer-payable LDs, penalties or termination fees anywhere. |
| 4 | T4C — Termination for convenience | High | Compliant | § 9.4 | Preferred position; 30 days' notice, partial termination, refund of prepaid Fees, no Vendor convenience right. |
| 5 | AUDIT — Audit rights against Customer | Medium | Compliant | § 22.1 (with §§ 22.2–22.3) | Preferred position on every material term, including 5% cost-shift trigger and no direct system access. |
| 6 | GOVLAW — Governing law and venue | Medium | Compliant | § 28.1 (with §§ 28.2–28.3) | New York law, New York County courts; no arbitration provision. |
| 7 | **INDEMN — Indemnification by Vendor** | Medium | **Deviation** | § 20 (§ 20.1) | Walk-away: one-way unlimited Customer indemnity, no Vendor indemnity at all; § 9.3 cross-refers to a non-existent § 20.5. |
| 8 | **LICENSE — Licence grant scope** | Medium | **Deviation** | § 13.1 | Walk-away: Customer only, Affiliates and contractors excluded, revocable at Vendor's sole discretion; conflicts with § 13.3. |
| 9 | **LOL-CAP — Liability cap, mutuality, carve-outs** | Medium | **Deviation** | § 21.1 | Walk-away twice over: cap of one month's Fees paid, and "without exception" overrides the § 21.3 Excluded Claims. |
| 10 | MFN — MFN obligations burdening Customer | Medium | Compliant | § 12.3 | No MFN or most-favoured-customer obligation on us; § 12.3 affirmatively confirms this. |
| 11 | NOSOLICIT — Non-solicitation binding Customer | Medium | Compliant | § 12.3 | No non-solicit or no-hire covenant; general recruitment expressly preserved. |
| 12 | RENEWAL — Auto-renewal and notice window | Medium | Compliant | § 8.2 (with § 8.3) | 12-month renewals, 30-day opt-out, 60-day reminder with deadline extension, CPI/3% uplift cap. |
| 13 | **TRANSITION — Transition assistance and data return** | Medium | **Deviation** | § 11.1 | Walk-away: immediate cessation of assistance and permanent deletion, no export; contradicts §§ 11.2–11.3. |
| 14 | **EXCLUSIVITY — Exclusivity binding Customer** | Low | **Deviation** | § 2.2 | Walk-away: sole and exclusive supplier for the full three-year term, no category limit, no performance exit; conflicts with § 12.3. |
| 15 | INSURANCE — Vendor insurance | Low | Compliant | § 18.1 (with § 18.2) | Preferred position on all limits; employer's liability is additional cover in our favour. |
| 16 | **MINCOMMIT — Minimum purchase commitments** | Low | **Deviation** | § 2.1 | Walk-away: three-year USD 2,000,000/year take-or-pay "without reduction or termination rights"; conflicts with §§ 9.4 and 12.3. |
| 17 | **NONCOMPETE — Non-compete on Customer** | Low | **Deviation** | § 12.4 | Walk-away: 24 months post-term, any competing product, any territory, no internal-development or acquisition carve-out; conflicts with § 12.3. |
| 18 | **WARRANTY — Performance warranty and duration** | Low | **Deviation** | § 19.2 | 15-day Deliverable warranty below the fallback and its cut-off extinguishes §§ 19.1 and 19.4 remedies; barely exceeds the § 6.1 acceptance window. |

---

## 3. Walk-away items

The following seven provisions are identified in the findings as walk-away positions under the playbook. They fail both the preferred and the fallback positions on material terms and should be treated as conditions of signature rather than trading chips.

1. **§ 2.1 — Take-or-pay minimum commitment.** Three-year, USD 2,000,000 per year, expressly without reduction or termination rights. Our position: Fees for Services ordered or used only, with no minimum or shortfall obligation. Fallback available in negotiation: a single 12-month commitment, reducible on 30 days' notice, with a true-up rather than a penalty.
2. **§ 2.2 — Sole-source exclusivity.** Full-term exclusivity with no category limit and no exit for service-level or delivery failure. Our position: convert the appointment to non-exclusive, aligning § 2.2 with § 12.3.
3. **§ 12.4 — Post-term non-compete on Customer.** 24 months post-term, any competing product or service, any territory, and it expressly bars acquisitions. Our position: delete. Fallback: named competing product, term only, 12-month cap, with internal-development and acquisition carve-outs.
4. **§ 13.1 — Services licence.** Customer alone, Affiliates and contractors excluded with no path to add them, revocable at Vendor's sole discretion. Our position: extend to Affiliates and contractors acting on our behalf, tie revocation to the § 13.3 notice-and-cure standard, and permit successor transfer via § 24.
5. **§ 20 — Indemnification.** No Vendor indemnity anywhere in the Agreement, coupled with an unlimited Customer indemnity for "every claim" relating to our use of the Services. Our position: add the Vendor indemnity (IP infringement, breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused Customer Data incidents, gross negligence and wilful misconduct), narrow our indemnity to Customer-provided content and our breach of law, add notice/control/cooperation procedure and the missing § 20.5 procure/modify/replace/refund remedies.
6. **§ 21.1 — Liability cap.** One month of Fees actually paid, applying "without exception" so that indemnities, confidentiality, data protection and security, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement all sit inside a one-month cap. Our position: the greater of 12 months' Fees paid or payable and USD 1,000,000, delete "without exception" so the § 21.3 Excluded Claims operate uncapped, and keep payment obligations outside the damages exclusion.
7. **§ 11.1 — Post-termination.** Immediate cessation of all assistance and permanent deletion of Customer Data with no export or migration support, directly contradicting §§ 11.2–11.3. Our position: up to six months of transition assistance at Vendor's then-current rates, with deletion subordinated to §§ 11.2–11.3; 90 days is an acceptable fallback.

**Not walk-away, but must move:** § 19.2. We are seeking a longer Deliverable conformance period and deletion of the correction/refund cut-off, with a non-limitation cross-reference preserving §§ 19.1, 19.3 and the § 6.2 / § 19.4 remedies.

---

## 4. Next steps

1. **Confirm the redline set before it goes out.** The proposed edits for the exclusivity (§ 2.2), minimum commitment (§ 2.1), non-compete (§ 12.4) and indemnity (§ 20) findings were repaired during verification and should be read once more in context. The proposed edits for the licence (§ 13.1), liability cap (§ 21.1), transition (§ 11.1) and warranty (§ 19.2) findings did not verify and require manual drafting before issue.
2. **Settle the warranty ask internally.** The finding rationale supports extending § 19.2 to 90 days, while the drafted proposal states 12 months for software with 90 days for Services. We should fix a single number before sending the markup.
3. **Use the internal contradictions in the cover note.** For §§ 2.1, 2.2 and 12.4 we can point to Vendor's own acknowledgement in § 12.3 that we have made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume or no-hire commitment; for § 11.1 to §§ 11.2–11.3; for § 13.1 to § 13.3; and for § 21.1 to § 21.3. Note that the order-of-precedence clause does not resolve conflicts internal to the Agreement, so each must be fixed on its face.
4. **Raise the drafting defects.** Renumber the duplicate § 2.2, and correct or supply the § 20.5 remedies on which § 9.3 depends.
5. **Brief the business owner on the walk-away list.** Items 1–7 above are gating; we should confirm the commercial team's appetite on the take-or-pay and exclusivity items before the first negotiation call, since those two drive the economics of the deal.
6. **Leave the compliant clauses alone.** The IP, assignment, convenience-termination, audit, governing law, renewal, insurance, MFN and non-solicit provisions meet the playbook and, in several cases, favour us. We will not reopen them.
"}
